lessonTitle: Thermal Energy Storage: Sensible and Latent Stores

blocks.text: A district-heating plant in northern Europe stores summer solar heat in a 50 000 m$^3$ insulated water pit and draws it down in January. A packaging factory in Spain instead keeps its chilled-water supply at exactly 7 $^\circ$C overnight with tanks of frozen salt-hydrate. Both are thermal stores; one holds heat as a temperature rise, the other as a change of phase, and their characteristics are very different.

blocks.markdown: Thermal energy storage decouples the time of heat supply from the time of heat demand. There are two basic mechanisms. In **sensible storage** the store material changes temperature without changing phase, and the energy stored is proportional to the temperature change. In **latent storage** the material absorbs or releases heat at a nearly constant temperature while it melts or freezes, and the energy stored is proportional to the latent heat of fusion.

blocks.title: Sensible heat storage
blocks.text: For a store of mass $m$ (kg) with specific heat $c_p$ (J/kg K) heated from $T_1$ to $T_2$, the stored energy is $Q=mc_p(T_2-T_1)$ (J). Divide by $3.6\times10^6$ to convert joules to kWh.

blocks.title: Energy stored in a hot-water tank
blocks.prompt: A 2.0 m$^3$ water tank (mass 2000 kg, $c_p=4180$ J/kg K typical) is heated from 40 to 80 $^\circ$C. Find the stored energy in MJ and kWh, and the energy per unit volume.
blocks.answer: The tank stores 334.4 MJ (92.9 kWh), or 167 MJ/m$^3$. Doubling $\Delta T$ would double the energy.

blocks.markdown: For a phase-change material (PCM) heated through its melting point, there are three steps: heating the solid to the melting temperature $T_m$, melting at $T_m$ (absorbing the latent heat $L$, in J/kg), and heating the liquid above $T_m$. Each term uses the specific heat of the phase present. The capacity of the store therefore includes the latent heat, which is often the dominant term when the operating range is narrow.

blocks.caption: $c_s$, $c_l$ specific heats of solid and liquid; $T_1<T_m<T_2$

blocks.title: Capacity of a paraffin store
blocks.prompt: 500 kg of paraffin wax (typical: $T_m=58\,^\circ$C, $L=200$ kJ/kg, $c_s=2000$ J/kg K, $c_l=2200$ J/kg K, density 800 kg/m$^3$) is heated from 40 to 70 $^\circ$C. Compare its energy with 500 kg of water heated over the same 30 K.

steps.text: Energy per unit volume (PCM volume 0.625 m$^3$, water 0.50 m$^3$).

blocks.answer: The wax stores 131.2 MJ against 62.7 MJ for water, about 2.1 times as much per kilogram, and 1.7 times as much per cubic metre; the latent term alone is 76 % of the total.

rows: $mL$ plus sensible terms, mostly at one temperature
Energy density over a narrow range
Falls steadily as energy is withdrawn
Nearly constant at $T_m$ while the phase changes
Low conductivity, supercooling, cost, cycling stability
blocks.caption: Typical comparison; values vary with material.

blocks.markdown: The two types are compared on **energy density** (per unit mass or volume) and on **temperature stability**. Over a wide temperature range a sensible store may match a PCM: water stores $4.18\times20=84$ kJ/kg over a 20 K swing, while ice stores 334 kJ/kg at 0 $^\circ$C - about four times as much. If the demand is at a fixed temperature, such as chilled water or a controlled room, the PCM's constant discharge temperature is a major advantage, since a sensible store delivers energy over a falling temperature that may drop below the usable level.

blocks.title: What matters in selection
blocks.text: Choose the melting point close to the operating temperature, check that the temperature swing available is small enough that latent heat dominates, and assess conductivity and cycling stability. A PCM operated entirely below its melting point behaves as a sensible store with a small heat capacity.

items: Water has a high specific heat, cheap and safe, but a boiling limit and a low density of energy.
Rock or concrete has lower $c_p$ but can reach high temperatures and costs little.
Real stores also lose heat to the surroundings; the numbers above are gross capacities.

blocks.title: Count only the phases that occur
blocks.text: If the PCM never reaches $T_m$, there is no latent term. If it is only partly melted, the stored latent heat is $m_{melted}L$, so the fraction melted is $Q_{latent}/(mL)$.

points: Sensible storage energy is $Q=mc_p\Delta T$; latent storage includes $mL$ at the melting temperature plus sensible terms on either side.
Phase-change stores give a higher energy density over a narrow temperature range and discharge at a nearly constant temperature.
Sensible stores are simple and cheap but their delivery temperature falls as they discharge.
Selection depends on the temperature level, available swing, conductivity, cost and cycling stability.

questions.stem: A packed bed of 5000 kg of crushed rock (specific heat 880 J/kg K, typical) is heated from 30 degrees Celsius to 110 degrees Celsius by hot air. Find the stored thermal energy in kWh.
questions.explanation: The stored energy is m cp dT = 5000 x 880 x 80 = 352 MJ. Dividing by 3.6 MJ per kWh gives 97.8 kWh. Rock has a lower specific heat than water, so a larger mass is needed for the same energy.

questions.stem: A hot-water cylinder must store 10 kWh of thermal energy using a temperature rise of 35 K. Taking the specific heat of water as 4180 J/kg K, find the mass of water required in kg.
questions.explanation: The energy is 10 x 3.6 = 36 MJ. The mass is Q/(cp dT) = 36e6/(4180 x 35) = 246 kg, which is about 246 litres of water.

questions.stem: An ice store holds 200 kg of ice at 0 degrees Celsius. All the ice melts and the water is then warmed to 12 degrees Celsius. Take the latent heat of fusion as 334 kJ/kg and the specific heat of water as 4180 J/kg K. Find the total energy absorbed in MJ.
questions.explanation: Melting absorbs 200 x 334 000 = 66.8 MJ and warming the water absorbs 200 x 4180 x 12 = 10.03 MJ, so the total is 76.8 MJ (21.3 kWh). The latent term is 87 percent of the total.

questions.stem: A store contains 120 kg of paraffin (typical: melting temperature 48 degrees Celsius, latent heat 180 kJ/kg, solid specific heat 2100 J/kg K, liquid specific heat 2200 J/kg K). It is heated from 40 degrees Celsius to 55 degrees Celsius, passing through complete melting. Find the total energy stored in MJ.
questions.explanation: There are three terms: solid heating 120 x 2100 x 8 = 2.02 MJ, melting 120 x 180 000 = 21.6 MJ and liquid heating 120 x 2200 x 7 = 1.85 MJ. The total is 25.46 MJ, and 85 percent of it is latent heat.

questions.stem: A chilled-water application requires cooling delivered at a steady 7 degrees Celsius for eight hours. Which storage approach provides the more stable delivery temperature?

options.text: A phase-change store with a melting point near 7 degrees Celsius, because it absorbs heat at nearly constant temperature while melting
A chilled-water tank, because its temperature does not change as it warms
A rock bed, because it has a high specific heat
Neither, because all storage delivers at changing temperature

questions.correctOptionText: A phase-change store with a melting point near 7 degrees Celsius, because it absorbs heat at nearly constant temperature while melting

distractorRationale.b: A sensible store warms steadily as heat is absorbed, so the delivery temperature rises.
distractorRationale.c: Rock has lower specific heat than water and its temperature also changes as energy is exchanged.
distractorRationale.d: A PCM at its melting point is the exception: temperature stays nearly fixed during the phase change.

questions.explanation: During melting or freezing the temperature of a pure PCM stays close to its melting point, so energy is exchanged at a nearly fixed temperature. A sensible store must change temperature to store or release energy, so its delivery temperature drifts.

questions.stem: Water is heated through a 20 K temperature swing. Compared with the energy absorbed by melting the same mass of ice (334 kJ/kg), the sensible energy of water ($c_p=4.18$ kJ/kg K) is

options.text: About one quarter as large, 84 kJ/kg against 334 kJ/kg
About the same, because both are water

questions.correctOptionText: About one quarter as large, 84 kJ/kg against 334 kJ/kg

distractorRationale.b: The latent heat of melting ice (334 kJ/kg) exceeds the sensible heat over 20 K (84 kJ/kg).
distractorRationale.c: The same substance can have very different energy absorption in a phase change and in a 20 K swing.
distractorRationale.d: The ratio is about 4 to 1, not 100 to 1.

questions.explanation: Sensible energy is $4.18\times20=83.6$ kJ/kg while melting ice absorbs 334 kJ/kg, a ratio near 4. That ratio explains why latent stores can be much more compact when the temperature swing is small.

questions.stem: Two stores hold the same mass and are heated through the same temperature range, but store X is water and store Y is crushed rock with a specific heat of 880 J/kg K. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Store X holds about 4.75 times as much energy as store Y, because the ratio of specific heats is 4180/880
Both hold the same energy, because the mass and temperature range are equal
Store Y holds more energy, because rock is denser
Store X holds half as much energy as store Y

questions.correctOptionText: Store X holds about 4.75 times as much energy as store Y, because the ratio of specific heats is 4180/880

distractorRationale.b: Energy also depends on specific heat, which differs between the materials.
distractorRationale.c: Density does not enter $mc_p\Delta T$ when the mass is given.
distractorRationale.d: Water has the larger specific heat, so it holds more energy per kilogram.

questions.explanation: At fixed mass and $\Delta T$ the energy is proportional to $c_p$. Water at 4180 J/kg K has about 4.75 times the specific heat of rock at 880 J/kg K, so it stores 4.75 times as much per kilogram.

questions.stem: A 40 kg PCM block with a latent heat of 200 kJ/kg is held exactly at its melting temperature and absorbs 3.2 MJ. What fraction of the PCM has melted?

options.text: 40 %, because the latent capacity is 8 MJ and 3.2 MJ is 40 % of it
16 %, because 3.2/(40 x 200) uses the latent heat in kJ without conversion
80 %, because 3.2 MJ is divided by 4 MJ
100 %, because any absorbed energy melts the whole block

questions.correctOptionText: 40 %, because the latent capacity is 8 MJ and 3.2 MJ is 40 % of it

distractorRationale.b: This divides 3.2 MJ by 20 MJ; the latent capacity is 40 x 200 kJ = 8 MJ, giving 0.4.
distractorRationale.c: The total capacity is 8 MJ, not 4 MJ.
distractorRationale.d: The block is only partly melted unless it absorbs the full 8 MJ.

questions.explanation: The latent capacity is $mL=40\times200\,000=8.0$ MJ. At the melting temperature all absorbed energy goes into melting, so the melted fraction is 3.2/8.0 = 0.40, with the temperature staying at the melting point.

questions.stem: Explain how the energy stored in a phase-change store that is heated from below to above its melting point is calculated, and why neglecting the latent heat term would give a poor estimate for a small temperature range.
markingGuide: Three terms: heating the solid to $T_m$, melting with latent heat $mL$, heating the liquid above $T_m$
Uses the correct specific heat $c_s$ and $c_l$ for each phase
Notes that over a narrow range the sensible terms are small, so latent heat dominates (e.g. 80 % or more)
Concludes that neglecting latent heat would underestimate capacity several-fold
questions.explanation: The energy stored includes the large amount absorbed during melting, which does not appear as a temperature rise. Over a narrow temperature range the sensible terms are small, so ignoring latent heat would be a gross error.

questions.stem: Discuss when you would choose a phase-change store rather than a sensible hot-water store for a building application, and identify two practical limitations of the phase-change option.
markingGuide: PCM chosen when space is limited and temperature swing is small, because of higher energy density
PCM chosen when stable delivery temperature is needed (comfort cooling, chilled water)
Water chosen when temperature swing is large, cost is critical, or high power charge and discharge needed
Limitation: low thermal conductivity limits charge/discharge power; heat exchangers or fins needed
Limitation: supercooling, phase separation, corrosion, cycling degradation, higher material cost
questions.explanation: A PCM is attractive where the temperature window is narrow and volume is valuable, because latent heat provides a large store at a nearly fixed temperature. Its low conductivity and ageing problems limit power and lifetime, so water remains the default.
